title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts

paper.title: Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts
paper.abstract:
Abstract Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters.
Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts.
The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token.
We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations.
This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice.
MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts.
MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales. Code is available here .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been instrumental in scaling large language models (LLMs) to trillions of parameters and beyond ( Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . MoEs adopt a sparse conditional-computation paradigm, where each token activates only a subset of experts, or subnetworks. During pretraining, recent work has shown that MoEs can outperform their dense counterparts under matched total parameter counts, compute, and data budgets ( Li et al., 2026 ) . At inference, sparse activation allows computational cost to grow sublinearly with total parameters. Thanks to these advantages, MoEs have become a core architecture underlying model families such as DeepSeek ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , Kimi ( Team-Kimi, 2025 ; Team-Kimi, 2026 ) , and Qwen ( Team-Qwen, 2024b ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , among many others ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Abdin et al., 2024 ) . At the core of MoEs is the MoE layer, which consists of a router and E E experts, each implemented as a feedforward network (FFN). For each input token, the router selects K K experts ( K < E K<E ) for sparse activation ( Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . Building on this basic design, recent MoEs have increasingly adopted two notable architectural advances. The first is fine-grained expert segmentation ( Team-Kimi, 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Recent MoEs tend to use larger numbers of both total and activated experts, i.e., larger E E and K K . For example, at the same activation ratio K / E K/E , ( E , K ) = ( 64 , 8 ) (E,K)=(64,8) is often preferred over ( E , K ) = ( 8 , 1 ) (E,K)=(8,1) . Since there are ( E K ) \binom{E}{K} expert combinations, the latter yields richer routing space for more expressive token representations ( Elango et al., 2026 ) . The second advance is shared experts . Activated for every token, shared experts capture common knowledge that would otherwise be learned redundantly by routed experts. This allows routed ones to devote more capacity to specialization. The combination of the above architectural choices have become standard in modern MoEs ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Team-Qwen, 2024b ) . This work reexamines the interaction between these two trends from the angle of routing exploration . The goal of exploration is to search for alternative expert combinations during pretraining to identify (near-)optimal routes for each token. On the one hand, realizing the expressive potential of fine-grained expert segmentation requires exploring a combinatorially larger routing space within each MoE layer. For example, the number of expert subsets increases from 8 8 when ( E , K ) = ( 8 , 1 ) (E,K)=(8,1) to ( 64 8 ) ≈ 4.4 × 10 9 {64\choose 8}\approx 4.4\times 10^{9} with ( E , K ) = ( 64 , 8 ) (E,K)=(64,8) , i.e., several orders of magnitude increase. On the other hand, our analysis reveals an asymmetry during pretraining: shared experts dominate the learned token representations, leaving routed experts with less influence on the layer output. Consequently, even activating different routed experts only leads to limited variation in the learned features, making alternative routes harder to distinguish and thereby undermining the goal of exploration. This exploration dilemma has tangible consequences for shared-expert MoEs. To see this, we train matched MoE models with and without shared experts at 4 scales, ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. At each scale, we fix the total number of experts E E and vary the number of (total) activated experts K K over { 6 , 8 , 10 } \{6,8,10\} . A larger K K simultaneously increases model expressiveness and demands more strategic exploration due to enlarged routing space. As shown in Fig. 1 , shared experts no longer provide benefits over their non-shared counterparts as K K increases. More strikingly, the performance of shared-expert MoEs can even degrade as K K increases in Figs. 1(b) and 1(d) , suggesting that the inefficient exploration hinders realization of the additional expressiveness from larger K K . MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile the conflicting architecture designs above. It adaptively suppresses routed experts on a token basis, reducing the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. Technically, MirrorMoE is derived by mirroring the routing logits via sign negation, hence its name. As shown in Fig. 1 , MirrorMoE improves the performance of shared-expert MoEs and attains expressiveness gains from larger K K . In summary, our contributions are as follows: ❖ We identify an exploration dilemma in modern MoEs: the enlarged routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration, while shared experts make routing less explorative. As a result, the benefits of shared experts diminish as the routing space grows. ❖ We propose MirrorMoE , which adaptively shrinks the exploration space to reconcile competing demands above. MirrorMoE is conceptually simple, and its adaptivity is theoretically characterized. ❖ We demonstrate that MirrorMoE addresses the exploration dilemma across MoEs of different scales. On the 2.4B model, MirrorMoE improves pretraining and downstream performance by 0.67 and 1.64 points, respectively. Moreover, it enables shared-expert MoEs to consistently outperform their non-shared counterparts and restores the performance gains from increasing K K ; see Fig. 1 . (a) 100M (b) 498M (c) 625M (d) 2.4B Figure 1: Comparison of MoEs with and without shared experts (SE) and the proposed MirrorMoE. MirrorMoE consistently i) achieves the best performance, ii) realizes the expressiveness gains from larger K K , and iii) enables shared-expert MoEs to outperform their non-shared counterparts.

sections.heading: 1.1 Related work
sections.text: MoEs. Modern sparse MoEs originated with the sparsely gated MoE layer of Shazeer et al. (2017) and were extended to large-scale Transformers in e.g., Lepikhin et al. (2020) ; Fedus et al. (2022) . Later work focused on improving scalability, stability, and expert specialization. GLaM ( Du et al., 2022 ) demonstrated that sparse language models could scale beyond one trillion parameters, while ST-MoE ( Zoph et al., 2022 ) improved training stability. MoEs have since become widely adopted. Beyond those mentioned earlier, other representative examples include Gemma4, OLMoE and gpt-oss ( Team-Gemma, 2026 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ) . Across this development trajectory, two trends have clearly emerged: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. Tension between expressiveness and pretraining. A growing line of work shows that a model’s expressive capacity may not be readily realized without carefully designed training procedures ( Lion et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Jha and Reagen, 2026 ; Wei et al., 2025a ) . Within the context of MoEs, related evidence is provided by Jin et al. (2024) , which augments learnable experts with fixed zero, copy, and constant experts. Although standard FFN experts can, in principle, learn these operations, explicitly incorporating them still improves empirical performance. The benefit of directly defining these operations, rather than learning them through training, suggests that the available expressiveness may not be fully realized in practice. Our work further shows that the additional expressiveness provided by fine-grained expert segmentation is not naturally attained in shared-expert MoEs. Additional related work on MoE routing and systems is deferred to App. A due to limited space.

sections.heading: 2 The Exploration Dilemma in Shared-Expert MoEs
sections.text: This section first reviews MoEs and then examines the effect of shared experts on exploration.

The models in this subsection have 121M activated and 498M total parameters, with E = 66 E=66 and K = 8 K=8 . sections.heading: 2.3 Consequences of the exploration dilemma
sections.text: The preceding discussions reveals a fundamental exploration dilemma in shared-expert MoEs. On the one hand, the combinatorial growth of the routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration to identify (near-)optimal expert combinations. On the other hand, shared experts reduce feature variation, thereby weakening exploration. This mismatch gives rise to several practical inefficiencies. We reveal them by evaluating models ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. We set R ∈ { 64,128 } R\in\{64,128\} and S = 2 S=2 for shared-expert MoEs, and match the total number of experts for MoEs without shared experts. We vary the number of activated experts as K ∈ { 6 , 8 , 10 } K\in\{6,8,10\} . In this scenario, increasing K K improves expressiveness but also enlarges the exploration space. Inefficiency 1. Benefits of shared experts are eroded. The first consequence is that shared-expert MoEs do not consistently improve upon standard MoEs. As shown in Fig. 1 , when K K is small and hence demanding less exploration, shared-expert MoEs outperform their non-shared counterparts. As K K increases, however, the benefits of shared experts diminish or even disappear. Inefficiency 2. Shared experts can diminish the expressive benefits of increasing K K . Across the four model scales in Fig. 1 , increasing K K from 6 6 to 10 10 yields perplexity gains of { 2.23 , 1.32 , \{2.23,1.32, 1.08 , 0.87 } 1.08,0.87\} for MoEs without shared experts. With shared experts, however, these gains drop to { 0.29 , − 0.03 , 0.58 , − 0.03 } \{0.29,-0.03,0.58,-0.03\} , i.e., negative at two scales. These negative numbers indicate that additional expressiveness from activating more experts is not fully realized with shared experts. Inefficiency 3. Shared experts slow routing specialization. As shown in Fig. 3(a) , replacing the learned router with a uniformly random one leads to a steadily increasing relative perplexity gap across training stages for MoEs without shared experts. This is expected as routing becomes increasingly specialized. In contrast, shared-expert MoEs exhibit little increase in this gap between the 20 % 20\% and 50 % 50\% checkpoints, suggesting slower routing specialization.

sections.heading: 3 MirrorMoE for Pretraining Shared-Expert MoEs
sections.text: To reconcile this exploration dilemma and mitigate the inefficiencies discussed earlier, we propose MirrorMoE, a simple yet effective pretraining approach tailored to MoEs with shared experts.

sections.heading: 3.1 MirrorMoE shrinks the exploration space
sections.text: One solution to the exploration dilemma is to encourage exploration. However, this can introduce tradeoffs in MoE training, such as reduced stability and increased optimization variance, as further illustrated in App. B.3 . We thus take the opposite approach: shrink the routing space to better match the model’s exploration capability. An intuitive way to view this is through the number of effective expert combinations, which scales with ( R K 𝖾𝖿𝖿 ) {R\choose K_{\mathsf{eff}}} . We formally define K 𝖾𝖿𝖿 K_{\mathsf{eff}} in Sec. 3.2 ; for now, it can be understood as the number of functionally active experts induced by the routing method. The routing space is reduced when K 𝖾𝖿𝖿 < K − S K_{\mathsf{eff}}<K-S . However, as shown by the ablation in Sec. 4.3 , naively reducing activated experts is suboptimal. MirrorMoE reduces K 𝖾𝖿𝖿 K_{\mathsf{eff}} by leveraging experts with low routing probabilities. It selects these low-probability experts in a token-adaptive manner but assigns them negligible aggregation weights. They therefore contribute little to the learned token representation and are functionally suppressed, reducing the number of experts that need to be explored. We detail this approach below. sections.heading: 3.3 Discussions on adaptivity of MirrorMoE
sections.text: Lastly, we theoretically characterize the adaptivity of MirrorMoE by deriving sufficient conditions for both expert suppression and preservation at mirror routing. We begin with the former. When an expert has a sufficiently small ξ l , e \xi_{l,e} and ρ \rho is chosen appropriately, MirrorMoE activates this expert but functionally removes it as negligible aggregation weight is assigned. For convenience, we omit the layer index throughout this subsection. Proposition 3.2 (Sufficient condition for expert suppression) . For a given token, let { ξ e } \{\xi_{e}\} and { p e } \{p_{e}\} be probabilities obtained as ( 3 ). Let 𝒜 p := 𝒜 {\cal A}^{p}:={\cal A} , i.e., ( 4 ), denote the set of experts activated by MirrorMoE, and define 𝒜 ξ := 𝖳𝗈𝗉 K − S ​ ( { ξ e } e = 1 R ) {\cal A}^{\xi}:=\mathsf{Top}_{K-S}(\{\xi_{e}\}_{e=1}^{R}) as the set that would be activated under the standard routing probabilities { ξ e } \{\xi_{e}\} . Let e min := arg ⁡ min e ∈ [ R ] ⁡ ξ e e_{\min}:=\arg\min_{e\in[R]}\xi_{e} with ξ e min = ϵ \xi_{e_{\min}}=\epsilon , and let j := arg ⁡ min e ∈ 𝒜 ξ ⁡ ξ e j:=\arg\min_{e\in{\cal A}^{\xi}}\xi_{e} with ξ j = c / R \xi_{j}=c/R . As ϵ → 0 \epsilon\to 0 , ρ > c / ( 1 + c ) \rho>c/(1+c) is sufficient for e min ∈ 𝒜 p ∖ 𝒜 ξ e_{\min}\in{\cal A}^{p}\setminus{\cal A}^{\xi} ; that is, MirrorMoE activates this expert while functionally suppressing its contribution during aggregation. This explains the reduced K 𝖾𝖿𝖿 K_{\mathsf{eff}} as visualized in Fig. 4 . Next, we show the token adaptivity of MirrorMoE by identifying a regime in which no expert is suppressed. Specifically, when the router is uncertain about its choices, MirrorMoE behaves similarly to standard routing. Proposition 3.3 (Sufficient condition for expert preservation) . Let ξ max := max e ∈ [ R ] ⁡ ξ e \xi_{\max}:=\max_{e\in[R]}\xi_{e} , ξ min := min e ∈ [ R ] ⁡ ξ e \xi_{\min}:=\min_{e\in[R]}\xi_{e} , and κ := ( 1 − ρ ) / ρ \kappa\!:=\!\sqrt{(1-\rho)/\rho} . If ξ max / ξ min ≤ κ \xi_{\max}/\xi_{\min}\leq\kappa , 𝒜 p = 𝒜 ξ {\cal A}^{p}\!=\!{\cal A}^{\xi} . Moreover, with ξ ¯ e \bar{\xi}_{e} defined in Def. 3.1 , it satisfies ξ ¯ e ≥ 1 / ( ( K − S ) ​ κ ) , ∀ e ∈ 𝒜 p \bar{\xi}_{e}\geq 1/((K\!-\!S)\kappa),\forall e\in{\cal A}^{p} , i.e., no selected expert is functionally suppressed. Another interpretation for MirrorMoE. The above discussions provide an alternative interpretation of MirrorMoE beyond exploration. In MoEs with large E E and K K , not every token may require the full expressiveness from all activated experts. If a token can be learned well using fewer experts, the capacity of remaining experts can be devoted to other tokens. MirrorMoE can therefore be viewed as an approach for tokens to adaptively determine their number of activated experts, where this adaptivity arises from the expert suppression and preservation shown in Props. 3.2 and 3.3 , respectively.

sections.heading: 4.2 Comparison under enlarged routing space
sections.text: Building on the same model configuration, we vary the number of activated experts as K ∈ { 6 , 8 , 10 } K\in\{6,8,10\} . Increasing K K enables richer expert combinations, thereby enlarging both the exploration space and model expressiveness. As shown in Fig. 1 , the standard shared-expert MoE is outperformed by its non-shared counterpart at large K K . In contrast, MirrorMoE mitigates the exploration dilemma, enabling the shared-expert model to consistently outperform the non-shared MoE across all tested cases. More importantly, the perplexity of MirrorMoE consistently decreases as K K increases, suggesting that the additional expressiveness enabled by larger K K is realized.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: This work identifies an exploration dilemma in MoEs that combine fine-grained expert segmentation with shared experts. This tension can prevent the additional expressiveness enabled by fine-grained segmentation from being fully realized while also diminishing the benefits of shared experts. To address this, we propose MirrorMoE, which adaptively shrinks the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across scales. Future direction. Our current approach addresses the exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space. A promising future direction is to improve the routing strategy itself for more efficient exploration.

sections.heading: Appendix A Additional related work
sections.text: Expressiveness does not necessarily translate directly into performance. Beyond those we have discussed earlier in Sec. 1.1 , additional works similarly suggest that the expressive capacity of neural networks may not be fully utilized in practice. For example, [ Csordás et al., 2025 ] shows that many deeper layers in Llama 3.1 70B behave close to identity mappings. Since identity mappings are available “for free”, this motivates redesign of residual connections for scaling deeper [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] . MoE systems. A complementary line of work focuses on efficient MoE systems, including faster and more principled expert parallelism, fine-grained all-to-all communication, and topology-aware communication strategies; see e.g., [ Hwang et al., 2023 , Liu et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025 ] . These methods aim to improve hardware utilization, communication efficiency, and end-to-end throughput. MirrorMoE is largely orthogonal to these system-level optimizations and can be integrated with them. Routing in MoEs. A broad line of work studies alternative routing mechanisms for MoEs. Hash Layers [ Roller et al., 2021 ] use hash-based assignments, while BASE Layers [ Lewis et al., 2021 ] and expert-choice routing [ Zhou et al., 2022 ] promote balanced expert utilization through carefully designed token assignments, at the cost of not being strictly autoregressive. Clark et al. [2022] study scaling laws for routed models. Other approaches replace hard top- K K selection with differentiable routing mechanisms [ Muqeeth et al., 2023 , Wang et al., 2025 , Vahidi et al., 2026 ] . Several works post-train or fine-tune routers to enable token-adaptive computation [ Yue et al., 2024 , Zeng et al., 2024 ] , while Kang [2025] uses reinforcement learning to improve routing decisions. During pretraining, noisy routing has also been explored to encourage broader expert exploration: Shazeer et al. [2017] introduce Gaussian noise, whereas Nie et al. [2021] use Gumbel noise. Routing has also been explicitly studied for multimodal models [ Wei et al., 2025b ] . In contrast to approaches that encourage broader exploration, MirrorMoE adaptively suppresses experts to shrink the exploration space. The work of Liang et al. [2026] studies shared experts from an inference perspective, showing that they can hinder expert offloading, partly because shared experts reduce the importance of routed experts. However, their focus is on routing behavior at inference time, whereas we study how shared experts affect routing throughout pretraining.

sections.heading: B.1 Training details
sections.text: The model configurations for the shared-expert MoE baseline and MirrorMoE are summarized in Tab. 4 . Following Kang et al. [2025] , we adopt a Llama-style MoE architecture. We also follow DeepSeekMoE [ Dai et al., 2024 , Liu et al., 2024 ] by using a dense FFN in the first Transformer layer, so that the first sparse layer receives sufficiently developed token representations for routing. MoE-100M-A38M is trained on two H100 GPUs, while all other models are trained on four. DCLM dataset [ Li et al., 2024 ] is adopted. We use AdamW for optimization. The learning rate is selected from { 1 , 3 , 5 } × 10 − 4 \{1,3,5\}\times 10^{-4} based on performance after 500 training steps on a held-out validation set. We adopt a warmup-stable-decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule. The global batch size is 1024 1024 , with gradient accumulation used to reduce memory consumption. The model analyzed in Sec. 2.2 is MoE-498M-A121M. For MoEs without shared experts, we convert the shared experts into routed experts to preserve the same total parameter count. Due to implementation constraints in Megatron-LM, this requires a different expert layout across GPUs, i.e., a different expert-parallelism configuration, and consequently a different number of GPUs. Specifically, Megatron-LM requires the number of routed experts to be divisible by the expert-parallelism size. Therefore, configurations with 66 or 130 routed experts use three or five GPUs, respectively. The global batch size consequently differs across configurations, while the total number of training tokens is kept approximately the same to ensure a fair comparison.

sections.heading: B.3 Increasing Exploration during Pretraining Can Be Tricky
sections.text: An alternative way to address the exploration dilemma is to encourage greater exploration during pretraining. However, this can be challenging for MoEs because stochastic routing may introduce unstable router dynamics and increased training variance. To examine this tradeoff, we consider two alternative routing strategies under K = 8 K=8 . First, we replace deterministic top- ( K − S ) (K-S) routing with stochastic sampling of K − S K-S experts, denoted as Sto- ( K − S ) (K-S) in Tab. 5 . Second, we deterministically select the top- 2 2 experts and stochastically sample the remaining K − S − 2 K-S-2 experts, denoted as Top- 2 2 + Sto- ( K − S − 2 ) (K-S-2) . As shown in Tab. 5 , on a MoE-100M-A38M model, deterministic top- ( K − S ) (K-S) routing performs best, followed by Top- 2 2 +Sto- ( K − S − 2 ) (K-S-2) , while fully stochastic routing performs worst. These results suggest that the additional instability introduced by exploration can outweigh its potential benefits during pretraining. For this reason, MirrorMoE takes the opposite approach by shrinking the exploration space. sections.heading: B.7 Comparison with top- p p routing
sections.text: We additionally compare MirrorMoE with another adaptive routing approach, namely top- p p routing [ Huang et al., 2024 ] . Top- p p routing activates the smallest set of experts whose cumulative probability exceeds p p , where p ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) p\in(0,1) is a threshold parameter. Intuitively, it also adapts the number of activated experts over training. Early in training, when routing probabilities are relatively uniform, more experts are required to exceed the threshold p p . As routing becomes more concentrated, fewer experts are sufficient. However, this adaptivity makes a fair comparison challenging. In our experiments, we observe that the average number of activated experts per token decreases over the course of training. As a result, top- p p routing uses different amounts of activated computation at different training stages, making direct comparison with MirrorMoE and the baseline difficult, as both use a fixed number of activated experts. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-SA 4.0 arXiv:2610.22353v1 [cs.LG] 15 Oct 2026 Rethinking Routing Exploration in Modern Mixture-of-Experts Bingcong Li 1,2 Hao Ma 2 Michael Muehlebach 3,4 Niao He 1 Yi Ma 2 Abstract Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have become an important approach for scaling model parameters. Modern MoE architectures increasingly combine two design choices: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. The former increases expressiveness by enabling more expert combinations at a fixed activation ratio, and the latter introduces experts that are active for every token. We identify an exploration dilemma between these designs: shared experts can make routing less exploratory by reducing the variability of token representations. This conflicts with the greater need for exploration induced by fine-grained expert segmentation due to the combinatorially enlarged routing space. Consequently, the additional expressiveness offered by fine-grained segmentation may not be fully realized in practice. MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile this exploration dilemma by shrinking the exploration space through token-adaptive suppression of unnecessary experts. MirrorMoE consistently improves performance across model scales. Code is available here . 1 ETH Zurich 2 The University of Hong Kong 3 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems 4 WU Vienna {bingcong.li, niao.he}@inf.ethz.ch, {haoma, mayi}@hku.hk, michael.muehlebach@tuebingen.mpg.de 1 Introduction Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models have been instrumental in scaling large language models (LLMs) to trillions of parameters and beyond ( Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . MoEs adopt a sparse conditional-computation paradigm, where each token activates only a subset of experts, or subnetworks. During pretraining, recent work has shown that MoEs can outperform their dense counterparts under matched total parameter counts, compute, and data budgets ( Li et al., 2026 ) . At inference, sparse activation allows computational cost to grow sublinearly with total parameters. Thanks to these advantages, MoEs have become a core architecture underlying model families such as DeepSeek ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , Kimi ( Team-Kimi, 2025 ; Team-Kimi, 2026 ) , and Qwen ( Team-Qwen, 2024b ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , among many others ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Abdin et al., 2024 ) . At the core of MoEs is the MoE layer, which consists of a router and E E experts, each implemented as a feedforward network (FFN). For each input token, the router selects K K experts ( K < E K<E ) for sparse activation ( Lepikhin et al., 2020 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ) . Building on this basic design, recent MoEs have increasingly adopted two notable architectural advances. The first is fine-grained expert segmentation ( Team-Kimi, 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . Recent MoEs tend to use larger numbers of both total and activated experts, i.e., larger E E and K K . For example, at the same activation ratio K / E K/E , ( E , K ) = ( 64 , 8 ) (E,K)=(64,8) is often preferred over ( E , K ) = ( 8 , 1 ) (E,K)=(8,1) . Since there are ( E K ) \binom{E}{K} expert combinations, the latter yields richer routing space for more expressive token representations ( Elango et al., 2026 ) . The second advance is shared experts . Activated for every token, shared experts capture common knowledge that would otherwise be learned redundantly by routed experts. This allows routed ones to devote more capacity to specialization. The combination of the above architectural choices have become standard in modern MoEs ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Team-Qwen, 2024b ) . This work reexamines the interaction between these two trends from the angle of routing exploration . The goal of exploration is to search for alternative expert combinations during pretraining to identify (near-)optimal routes for each token. On the one hand, realizing the expressive potential of fine-grained expert segmentation requires exploring a combinatorially larger routing space within each MoE layer. For example, the number of expert subsets increases from 8 8 when ( E , K ) = ( 8 , 1 ) (E,K)=(8,1) to ( 64 8 ) ≈ 4.4 × 10 9 {64\choose 8}\approx 4.4\times 10^{9} with ( E , K ) = ( 64 , 8 ) (E,K)=(64,8) , i.e., several orders of magnitude increase. On the other hand, our analysis reveals an asymmetry during pretraining: shared experts dominate the learned token representations, leaving routed experts with less influence on the layer output. Consequently, even activating different routed experts only leads to limited variation in the learned features, making alternative routes harder to distinguish and thereby undermining the goal of exploration. This exploration dilemma has tangible consequences for shared-expert MoEs. To see this, we train matched MoE models with and without shared experts at 4 scales, ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. At each scale, we fix the total number of experts E E and vary the number of (total) activated experts K K over { 6 , 8 , 10 } \{6,8,10\} . A larger K K simultaneously increases model expressiveness and demands more strategic exploration due to enlarged routing space. As shown in Fig. 1 , shared experts no longer provide benefits over their non-shared counterparts as K K increases. More strikingly, the performance of shared-expert MoEs can even degrade as K K increases in Figs. 1(b) and 1(d) , suggesting that the inefficient exploration hinders realization of the additional expressiveness from larger K K . MirrorMoE is proposed to reconcile the conflicting architecture designs above. It adaptively suppresses routed experts on a token basis, reducing the exploration space to better match the model’s exploration capability. Technically, MirrorMoE is derived by mirroring the routing logits via sign negation, hence its name. As shown in Fig. 1 , MirrorMoE improves the performance of shared-expert MoEs and attains expressiveness gains from larger K K . MirrorMoE is conceptually simple, and its adaptivity is theoretically characterized. ❖ We demonstrate that MirrorMoE addresses the exploration dilemma across MoEs of different scales. On the 2.4B model, MirrorMoE improves pretraining and downstream performance by 0.67 and 1.64 points, respectively. Moreover, it enables shared-expert MoEs to consistently outperform their non-shared counterparts and restores the performance gains from increasing K K ; see Fig. 1 . Modern sparse MoEs originated with the sparsely gated MoE layer of Shazeer et al. (2017) and were extended to large-scale Transformers in e.g., Lepikhin et al. (2020) ; Fedus et al. (2022) . Later work focused on improving scalability, stability, and expert specialization. GLaM ( Du et al., 2022 ) demonstrated that sparse language models could scale beyond one trillion parameters, while ST-MoE ( Zoph et al., 2022 ) improved training stability. MoEs have since become widely adopted. Beyond those mentioned earlier, other representative examples include Gemma4, OLMoE and gpt-oss ( Team-Gemma, 2026 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ) . Across this development trajectory, two trends have clearly emerged: fine-grained expert segmentation and shared experts. Tension between expressiveness and pretraining. A growing line of work shows that a model’s expressive capacity may not be readily realized without carefully designed training procedures ( Lion et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Jha and Reagen, 2026 ; Wei et al., 2025a ) . Within the context of MoEs, related evidence is provided by Jin et al. (2024) , which augments learnable experts with fixed zero, copy, and constant experts. Although standard FFN experts can, in principle, learn these operations, explicitly incorporating them still improves empirical performance. The benefit of directly defining these operations, rather than learning them through training, suggests that the available expressiveness may not be fully realized in practice. Our work further shows that the additional expressiveness provided by fine-grained expert segmentation is not naturally attained in shared-expert MoEs. On the one hand, the combinatorial growth of the routing space induced by fine-grained expert segmentation demands greater exploration to identify (near-)optimal expert combinations. On the other hand, shared experts reduce feature variation, thereby weakening exploration. This mismatch gives rise to several practical inefficiencies. We reveal them by evaluating models ranging from 100M to 2.4B total parameters. Another interpretation for MirrorMoE. The above discussions provide an alternative interpretation of MirrorMoE beyond exploration. In MoEs with large E E and K K , not every token may require the full expressiveness from all activated experts.
